```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
using CairoMakie, CEVE543Utils, CSV, DataFrames, Distributions, LaTeXStrings, Printf, Random, Statistics, Turing

set_theme!(theme_minimal(); fontsize=20)
colors = Makie.wong_colors()
```

## The data

```{julia}
#| output: false
here = @__DIR__
rng = MersenneTwister(543)

hobby = CSV.read(joinpath(here, "hobby-annmax.csv"), DataFrame)
hobby = hobby[hobby.n_valid_days .>= 350, :]     # the complete years
co2 = CSV.read(joinpath(here, "logCO2.csv"), DataFrame)
hobby = innerjoin(hobby, co2; on=:year)           # adds a log_CO2 column
y = hobby.prcp_mm
```

Houston Hobby annual maximum daily rainfall, `{julia} nrow(hobby)` years, and the natural log of atmospheric CO2 in parts per million.

# Choosing a covariate

## Hobby annual maxima against two covariates

```{julia}
#| echo: false
fig = Figure(; size=(1000, 280))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel="Year", ylabel="Annual max daily rainfall (mm)")
ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xlabel=L"\log(\text{CO}_2 \text{ in ppm})")
scatter!(ax1, hobby.year, y; color=colors[1], markersize=8)
scatter!(ax2, hobby.log_CO2, y; color=colors[1], markersize=8)
hideydecorations!(ax2; grid=false)
fig
```

::: {.callout-tip .pause}
## Think

Which covariate will fit better?
:::

## Over the record, year and log CO2 move together

- Correlation `{julia} @sprintf("%.2f", cor(hobby.year, hobby.log_CO2))`: a fit on this record cannot tell them apart.
- They differ once you extrapolate, which is where the choice matters.

## Choose a covariate by mechanism

The covariate-based recipe [@schlef_idf:2023, p. 8], where EVD is an extreme value distribution:

- "Determine suitable covariates based on causative mechanisms"
- "Fit an EVD, with parameters dependent on the covariates"
- "Create future projections by forcing the EVDs with projections of the covariates"

"Time, as a covariate, does not represent a mechanistic process" [@schlef_idf:2023, p. 9].

## Three kinds of covariate

Physical drivers used as covariates for extreme rainfall (from a paper in preparation in my group):

- **Thermodynamic:** temperature, such as global mean surface temperature.
- **Dynamical:** large-scale patterns that steer storms, such as El Niño (Niño 3.4).
- **External forcing:** CO2 concentration, used here and in Friday's lab.

## Which covariates published studies test

Of the 16 covariate-based rainfall studies in the review [@schlef_idf:2023, Table 1]:

- 12 test time, and 8 use nothing else.
- 6 test a climate index such as El Niño, and 4 test a temperature.
- None uses CO2.

## Kendall's $\tau$ as a covariate screen

Mann-Kendall's statistic is Kendall's $\tau$ between a record and the year.
Put a covariate in place of the year and the same statistic screens the covariate.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Figure shown in class: Kendall's rank correlation between smoothed global mean surface temperature and 1-hour (left) and 1-day (right) annual maximum rainfall at Texas stations with at least 60 years of record; blue is positive and red negative, and most stations are positive (preliminary, from a paper in preparation in my group).
:::

# Writing the model

## Centering and scaling the covariate

$$
x_t = \frac{\log \text{CO}_{2,t} - \overline{\log \text{CO}_2}}{s_{\log \text{CO}_2}}
$$

```{julia}
#| output: false
x_center, x_scale = mean(hobby.log_CO2), std(hobby.log_CO2)
x = (hobby.log_CO2 .- x_center) ./ x_scale
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# params gives the intercept at the covariate's mean; this moves it back to zero
function uncentered_intercept(covariate)
    β = params(gevfit(y; locationcov=[covariate])).β_location
    return β[1] - β[2] * mean(covariate)
end
raw_intercept_year = uncentered_intercept(hobby.year)
raw_intercept_co2 = uncentered_intercept(hobby.log_CO2)
```

- Uncentered, the intercept is the location at the year 0, or at 1 ppm of CO2: `{julia} round(Int, raw_intercept_year)` mm and `{julia} round(Int, raw_intercept_co2)` mm.
- Centered, the intercept is the location in an average year, and the slope is per standard deviation, so priors are easy to set.
- Centering also makes the optimizer and the sampler faster.

## A trend in the location

$$
y_t \sim \text{GEV}(\mu_0 + \mu_1 x_t, \sigma, \xi)
$$

```{julia}
#| output: false
@model function gev_location_trend(y, x)
    μ0 ~ Normal(100, 50)        # mm, in an average year of the record
    μ1 ~ Normal(0, 25)          # mm per standard deviation of x
    logσ ~ Normal(3, 2)
    ξ ~ Normal(0, 0.25)
    σ := exp(logσ)
    for t in eachindex(y)
        y[t] ~ GEVKernel(μ0 + μ1 * x[t], σ, ξ)
    end
end
location_model = gev_location_trend(y, x)
```

This is the week 4 model with $\mu$ replaced by a regression on $x_t$.

## Maximum likelihood fit of the location trend

```{julia}
start = InitFromParams((μ0=median(y), μ1=0.0, logσ=log(std(y)), ξ=0.1))
location_mle = maximum_likelihood(location_model; initial_params=start)
θ̂ = NamedTuple(location_mle.params)
@printf("μ0 = %.1f mm, μ1 = %.2f mm per sd, σ = %.1f mm, ξ = %.2f\n", θ̂.μ0, θ̂.μ1, θ̂.σ, θ̂.ξ)
```

## A trend in the location and the scale

$$
y_t \sim \text{GEV}\left(\mu_0 + \mu_1 x_t, \exp(\lambda_0 + \lambda_1 x_t), \xi\right)
$$

```{julia}
#| output: false
@model function gev_location_scale_trend(y, x)
    μ0 ~ Normal(100, 50)
    μ1 ~ Normal(0, 25)
    λ0 ~ Normal(3, 2)           # log scale in an average year; exp keeps the scale positive
    λ1 ~ Normal(0, 0.5)         # change in log scale per standard deviation of x
    ξ ~ Normal(0, 0.25)
    for t in eachindex(y)
        y[t] ~ GEVKernel(μ0 + μ1 * x[t], exp(λ0 + λ1 * x[t]), ξ)
    end
end
start = InitFromParams((μ0=median(y), μ1=0.0, λ0=log(std(y)), λ1=0.0, ξ=0.1))
both_mle = maximum_likelihood(gev_location_scale_trend(y, x); initial_params=start)
```

## Fitting the same models with gevfit

```{julia}
# gevfit centers and scales covariates itself; gevfitbayes takes the same keywords
fit_location = gevfit(y; locationcov=[hobby.log_CO2])
fit_both = gevfit(y; locationcov=[hobby.log_CO2], logscalecov=[hobby.log_CO2])
fit_year = gevfit(y; locationcov=[hobby.year])
@printf("location: %.2f, %.2f\n", location_mle.lp, loglike(fit_location))
@printf("both:     %.2f, %.2f\n", both_mle.lp, loglike(fit_both))
@printf("year:     %.2f\n", loglike(fit_year))
```

- Log likelihoods by hand and from `gevfit` match, and year gives the same fit as log CO2.

## The 100-year level under three models

```{julia}
#| echo: false
fits = ["stationary" => gevfit(y), "trend in location" => fit_location, "trend in location and scale" => fit_both]
fig = Figure(; size=(1000, 300))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel="Year", ylabel="Rainfall (mm)")
scatter!(ax, hobby.year, y; color=:gray, markersize=6, label="annual maximum")
for (k, (label, fit)) in enumerate(fits)
    lines!(ax, hobby.year, returnlevel(fit, 100); color=colors[k], linewidth=3, label=label)
end
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax; framevisible=false)
fig
```

Adding the scale trend raises the log likelihood by `{julia} @sprintf("%.1f", loglike(fit_both) - loglike(fit_location))` and moves the 2025 100-year level by `{julia} round(Int, last(returnlevel(fit_both, 100)) - last(returnlevel(fit_location, 100)))` mm.
Wednesday's reading makes the same comparison for Brays Bayou [@smith_brays:2026].

# Projecting

## Three CO2 paths to 2100

```{julia}
#| output: false
ppm_2025 = exp(last(co2.log_CO2))
recent_rate = (ppm_2025 - exp(co2.log_CO2[end - 10])) / 10     # ppm per year, 2015-2025
ppm_2100 = [
    "held at 2025" => ppm_2025, "last decade's rate" => ppm_2025 + 75recent_rate, "doubled" => 2ppm_2025,
]
```

The three paths span a range and are not published emissions scenarios.

## Year and log CO2 extrapolate differently

```{julia}
#| echo: false
future = 2025:2100
μ_year(yr) = first(params(fit_year).β_location) + last(params(fit_year).β_location) * (yr - mean(hobby.year))
μ_co2(logppm) = θ̂.μ0 + θ̂.μ1 * (logppm - x_center) / x_scale
fig = Figure(; size=(1000, 190))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel="Year", ylabel="Location change (mm)")
lines!(ax, future, μ_year.(future) .- μ_year(2025); color=:black, linewidth=3, label="trend in year")
for (k, (label, ppm_end)) in enumerate(ppm_2100)
    path = log.(range(ppm_2025, ppm_end; length=length(future)))
    lines!(ax, future, μ_co2.(path) .- μ_co2(log(ppm_2025)); color=colors[k], linewidth=3, label="log CO2, $label")
end
axislegend(ax; position=:lt)
fig
```

A trend in year gives one projection.
A trend in log CO2 gives a different projection for each CO2 path.

## Two sources of uncertainty in a projected level

Let $z$ be the 100-year level in 2100 and $s$ the CO2 path.
By the law of total variance,

$$
\mathrm{Var}(z) = \underbrace{E[\mathrm{Var}(z \mid s)]}_{\text{parameters}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}(E[z \mid s])}_{\text{CO2 path}}
$$

```{julia}
#| output: false
chain = sample(rng, location_model, NUTS(0.99), MCMCThreads(), 1_000, 4; progress=false)
draws = DataFrame(chain)
level_100yr(μ, σ, ξ) = quantile(GeneralizedExtremeValue(μ, σ, ξ), 1 - 1 / 100)
x_2100(ppm) = (log(ppm) - x_center) / x_scale
levels_2100 = [label => [level_100yr(d.μ0 + d.μ1 * x_2100(ppm), d.σ, d.ξ) for d in eachrow(draws)] for (label, ppm) in ppm_2100]
```

Weighting the three paths equally is itself an assumption.

## Most of the uncertainty comes from the parameters

```{julia}
#| echo: false
fig = Figure(; size=(900, 210))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel="100-year level in 2100 (mm)")
for (k, (label, z)) in enumerate(levels_2100)
    density!(ax, z; color=(colors[k], 0.3), strokecolor=colors[k], strokewidth=2, label=label)
end
hideydecorations!(ax)
axislegend(ax; position=:rt)
fig
```

```{julia}
var_parameters = mean(var(z) for (_, z) in levels_2100)
var_path = var([mean(z) for (_, z) in levels_2100]; corrected=false)
@printf("parameters %.0f mm², CO2 path %.0f mm², path share %.1f%%\n",
    var_parameters, var_path, 100var_path / (var_parameters + var_path))
```

## Every trend parameter costs precision in the tail

- Each coefficient is estimated from the same `{julia} nrow(hobby)` years, and its uncertainty carries into every return level.
- Without a covariate that represents a mechanism, "the more parsimonious stationary model should be assumed" (Serinaldi and Kilsby 2015, quoted in @schlef_idf:2023, p. 10).
- On Wednesday, the Brays Bayou 100-year interval widens when the trend parameters are added [@smith_brays:2026, p. 16].
